title: frontend tests accessibility browser automation and Playwright
concepts: Frontend tests should observe the interface as a user does: roles, labels, visible text, focus, keyboard behavior, and navigation. Implementation-specific selectors make refactors unnecessarily brittle.

Component tests verify rendering and interactions in a simulated DOM; browser tests exercise real browser behavior, routing, storage, layout, and network boundaries. Use each layer for the behavior it can represent reliably.
Async UI behavior requires waiting for the observable condition rather than sleeping for a guessed duration. Control timers, network responses, and state changes so failures are deterministic.
Accessibility testing combines semantic HTML, keyboard and assistive-technology behavior, automated rule checks, and human review. An automated scan detects only a subset of accessibility barriers.
Browser tests need clear ownership of browser contexts, test data, and cleanup. Parallel workers must not mutate the same account, record, or external environment.
Visual snapshots can reveal unexpected differences but require stable fonts, viewport, animation, and platform settings; approve intentional changes as part of code review.

accuracyFacts: Testing Library's getBy queries are synchronous and throw for zero or multiple matches; queryBy returns null for no match but throws for multiple matches; findBy queries retry asynchronously and reject if no unique match appears within the configured timeout.

Testing Library prioritizes queries reflecting accessible user experience, especially role/name and label queries. getByTestId is a fallback when semantic queries do not fit; it does not validate accessibility.

Testing Library's waitFor callback may run multiple times; assertions belong inside it, not side effects. Prefer findBy for waiting for a matching element and waitForElementToBeRemoved for disappearance.
user-event models higher-level user interactions and should be preferred for most interactions. fireEvent dispatches lower-level DOM events and can bypass parts of realistic interaction behavior.

Vitest fake timers affect timer APIs and may also affect time-related APIs such as Date or performance depending on current configuration/version; restore real timers and reset mock/global/environment state between tests.
MSW setupServer in Node.js intercepts requests in the process and does not open a real network server. It can share request handlers with browser-side MSW, subject to environment differences.

Playwright Test creates an isolated BrowserContext for each test by default; browser contexts isolate browser storage state such as cookies and local storage, but do not isolate external backend data or shared accounts.
Playwright locators auto-wait for actionability and web-first assertions retry until their condition passes or times out. Fixed sleeps should not be used as synchronization.
Playwright route interception and MSW both control API responses at different integration seams; neither proves the real backend's behavior.

Automated axe-core accessibility checks find only a subset of accessibility issues. Automated scans do not replace keyboard testing, assistive-technology testing, expert review, or evaluation against all applicable WCAG success criteria.
A WCAG 2.2 Level A or AA label refers to conformance requirements at that level, not an automatic guarantee from passing a particular tool scan.

Visual screenshot comparison is environment-sensitive; viewport, browser, fonts, device scale, animation, dynamic content, and color scheme affect results. A baseline update must be reviewed as a code change, not accepted automatically.

WCAG 2.2 conformance claims apply to full pages; Level A requires all Level A success criteria, and Level AA requires all Level A and Level AA criteria (or a conforming alternate version). An automated axe scan alone cannot establish either claim.
